paper_title: From Repositories to Training Environments: Scaling Long-Horizon Coding Agents with Environment Evolution Loop

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Training coding agents for long-horizon tasks requires environments with verifiable feedback. Existing pipelines often follow a linear process that ends with validation, establishing usability but providing little guidance on improving training value. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) often requires model rollouts or model training followed by downstream evaluation, with costs and feedback delays amplified on long-horizon tasks. How can we use timely, reliable proxy signals to improve training value and synthesize environments at scale? We present RepoFactory, an automated pipeline that converts real repositories into verifiable environments where agents build complete projects from scratch given a language specification. Its Environment Evolution Loop optimizes a multiplicative objective combining validity, structural coupling, and implementation scope through proxy feedback. RepoFactory produces 10,159 environments across 17 software domains. Training Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on these environments yields RepoHorizen-35B-A3B, which achieves gains of 22.6 percentage points on NL2Repo-Bench and 8.5 points on average across five benchmarks covering long-horizon coding and agentic tasks in real-world production settings, compared with 17.5 and 6.4 points without environment evolution. These results highlight the training value of RepoFactory environments and the additional gains from the Environment Evolution Loop.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being developed into agents that can carry out consequential work in real-world environments (Team et al., 2026a; Xu et al., 2026; Team, 2026; Yang et al., 2026a; DeepSeek-AI et al.). Unlike static language tasks, agentic work unfolds through sustained interaction with environments. This transition changes the objective of model training: capable agent must learn not only to produce correct answers, but also to make coherent progress toward completing long-horizon tasks (Li et al., 2026a; Tian et al., 2026; Bajoria et al., 2026). Software engineering has become major application of coding agents. Pipelines built around bug fixing and feature development have provided verifiable tasks for training agents on real codebases (Pan et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025). successful local change, however, is only part of the work involved in delivering software. Coding agents are increasingly expected to handle more complex development processes and produce complete, working systems (Yang et al., 2026c; Team et al., 2026b). Training on short-horizon tasks alone cannot cover this broader process, making it increasingly important to build repository-level environments for agent training. Constructing environments for long-horizon tasks at the repository level remains challenging. (i) Rigid construction pipelines limit the usable repository pool. DeNovoSWE (Zhao et al., 2026) and MindForge (Chen et al., 2026) follow linear construction pipelines. They refine documentation or resolve build failures while keeping the reference implementation fixed. Repositories that remain unsuitable are discarded, even when further revision could make them usable. Scaling therefore depends on finding more repositories that meet the same fixed requirements. (ii) Feedback focused on reliability overlooks training value. RefactorForge (Ebrahimi et al., 2026) and TrajLong (Peng et al., 2026a) design data for specific capabilities but do not explore how environment feedback can improve task content. ProgramGym (Yang et al., 2026b) uses execution diagnostics and coverage feedback to repair builds and strengthen tests around fixed reference implementation. These signals improve reliability without explicitly optimizing training value, which may remain limited when task requires little implementation work or coordination across components. (iii) Feedback from model execution is costly and time-consuming. BenchEvolver (Wu et al., 2026) and SETA (Shen et al., 2026) use model performance to guide task revision. Obtaining this feedback requires model rollouts on the candidate tasks. For long-horizon coding tasks, each rollout can involve extensive implementation, increasing computational costs and delaying subsequent revisions. How to obtain timely, reliable feedback at low cost to improve training value and synthesize long-horizon coding environments at scale remains an open research question. We present RepoFactory, an automated pipeline that transforms real-world repositories into verifiable environments. We design these environments around full repository generation task, in which an agent must build complete, functioning repository from scratch given language specification. We define multiplicative objective combining validity, structural coupling, and implementation scope. It provides timely feedback at low cost without requiring model to solve each candidate task. Our Environment Evolution Loop uses this objective to guide joint revisions to the oracle implementation, task specification, and tests. Validity feedback helps the loop repair initially unsuitable environments and recover repositories that would otherwise be discarded. Structural coupling and implementation scope serve as proxies for training value, directing revisions toward the implementation and integration work required by the task. construction agent chooses how to modify each candidate and receives updated measurements after each revision, iterating within fixed construction budget. Our main contributions are threefold: We introduce RepoFactory, an automated pipeline that converts real-world projects into 10,159 verifiable full-repository generation environments across 17 software domains. We develop an Environment Evolution Loop that optimizes multiplicative objective combining validity, structural coupling, and implementation scope. Timely, low-cost proxy feedback guides improvements to both environment reliability and training value. Training Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on RepoFactory yields RepoHorizen-35B-A3B, with gains of 22.6 percentage points on NL2Repo-Bench and 8.5 points on average across five coding and agentic benchmarks. Environment evolution contributes 5.1 and 2.1 points to these gains, respectively.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: 2.1 Scaling Verifiable Environments Environment synthesis scales agent training by generating interactive tasks with executable verification (Kulikov et al., 2026; Ren et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2025). EnvScaler (Song et al., 2026) and ScaleEnv (Tu et al., 2026) target tool use, while Endless Terminals (Gandhi et al., 2026), LiteCoder-Terminal (Peng et al., 2026b), and CLIUniverse (Hua et al., 2026) extend this approach to terminal-agent training. Broader task coverage, however, does not ensure that tasks preserve the interdependent requirements of real software or demand sustained development. RepoFactory derives full-repository generation tasks from real projects, grounding task behavior in existing implementations and tests. Reconstructing an entire repository requires sustained implementation and integration across these interdependent components. 2.2 Recursive Synthesis and Agent Self-Improvement Self-training reuses successful solutions as supervision, while self-play generates new problems for agents to solve (Chen et al., 2024; Li et al., 2026b). BenchEvolver (Wu et al., 2026) evolves reference solutions to construct harder tasks, while SETA (Shen et al., 2026) adapts terminal environments using learner performance. DataMaster (Du et al., 2026) optimizes training data using downstream evaluation scores, adding model training to the feedback cycle. These approaches rely on solver rollouts or downstream training, increasing computational costs and delaying feedback. To our knowledge, RepoFactory is the first to evolve full-repository generation environments using an objective that combines validity checks with inexpensive code metrics. This objective provides timely feedback without requiring solver rollouts or downstream training.

All three terms are evaluated on the current candidate. The Environment Evolution Loop iteratively revises the environment to maximize within fixed construction budget. 3.2 Construction Pipeline Repository Search and Filtering RepoFactory searches public code-hosting platforms for candidate repositories, excluding those included in established coding benchmarks to avoid evaluation overlap. Eligible projects must provide package metadata and nonempty local test suite to support isolated installation and evaluation. To balance task complexity with reconstruction cost, we require at least five implementation files and fewer than 40,000 lines of Python code. We exclude projects that require external services, outbound network access, graphical interfaces, or specialized hardware. Network-related projects remain eligible when their tests mock external calls or use only local connections. Runtime Construction and Repository Analysis For each candidate repository, RepoFactory copies each candidate repository into an isolated task directory and builds Docker image from its build files and dependency manifests. agent installs dependencies, identifies test commands, and revises the image or execution configuration as needed. We retain repository only when all tests pass in fresh container with bounded resources and no network access. RepoFactory archives the validated image and records the installation and test commands, package files, and test results. After establishing the runtime, RepoFactory analyzes the repository in read only container to determine what the task specification must cover. scanner based on abstract syntax trees extracts public classes, functions, and methods, together with their signatures, exceptions, and return information. It also records repository symbols imported by tests and builds an implementation tree excluding test files. These outputs guide task synthesis and, together with dependency metadata, provide the inputs for computing structural coupling and implementation scope. Task Synthesis and Environment Materialization. RepoFactory prepares an isolated workspace with dependencies installed and disabled external network access. The coding agent must reconstruct the project from the task specification, without access to the original repository or evaluation code. The synthesis agent uses the repository analysis to write this specification and an accompanying API manifest. The specification describes the repositorys functionality and structure, while the API manifest documents the public interfaces the agent must implement. Functionally correct implementations can still fail if their interface names or import paths differ from those expected by the tests. RepoFactory therefore checks the specification and API manifest against the repository symbols imported by the original tests, returning missing symbols and their import records to the synthesis agent for revision. Once this check passes, RepoFactory combines the specification with the validated runtime image to create the environment. The original repository remains isolated as the oracle, and evaluation resources are available only during verification. Environment Evolution Loop After materialization, RepoFactory first checks validity A. The oracle must receive full reward, and the unchanged initial workspace must receive zero reward. If either condition fails, the construction agent uses the validation report and execution trace to identify the cause and repair the candidate. The revised environment is evaluated again, and optimization of scope and coupling begins only after both checks pass. valid environment may still require little implementation work. Implementation scope therefore guides revisions toward more substantial reconstruction tasks. larger project can still consist of independent components, so structural coupling complements scope by directing evolution toward more interdependent functionality. The construction agent decides how to revise the oracle implementation, task specification, and tests, keeping the description and evaluation consistent with the revised functionality. For each valid candidate, the agent compares and against thresholds of 0.5 and 0.01, respectively, and prioritizes any term below threshold. When both thresholds are met, the agent chooses which term to optimize under Q. Each revision is rechecked for validity before the scores are reassessed, with validity failures returned to repair. revision targeting or is retained only if the selected score strictly increases; otherwise, RepoFactory restores the previous version. The loop runs for up to 12 rounds, assessing each revision through verifier execution and code analysis without solving-agent rollouts or downstream training and evaluation. RepoFactory uses this low-cost feedback to recover failed candidates and improve valid tasks, increasing both the yield and training value of repository-level environments.

sections.title: 4 Analysis of Synthesized Data
sections.content: Effective training environments for long-horizon coding should expose agents to diverse software and require substantial repository reconstruction under reliable feedback across broad range of difficulty. Our 10,159 RepoFactory environments span 17 domains and place agents in complete repository reconstruction tasks with executable validation. To collect SFT data, we run Qwen3.8-Max five times on each environment, filter out low reward trajectories, and retain 10,947 samples spanning 5,577 environments. We analyze the resulting Figure 2: Statistics of RepoFactory environments and SFT data. collection to characterize its diversity, scale, interaction length, and difficulty with the statistics summarized in Figure 2. Diversity. The collection covers broad range of application domains and technical ecosystems, without being dominated by any single area, as shown in Figure 2(a). The largest category accounts for only 12.5% of environments, and only 6.9% fall outside the named domains, indicating broad coverage rather than concentration. Its varied libraries, interfaces, and implementation conventions expose agents to the diversity of real software development. This breadth supports training agents that generalize across software projects instead of specializing in narrow domain. Scale and verification. These environments require agents to reconstruct substantial codebases rather than write isolated programs. As shown in Figure 2(b), the median oracle contains 4.2k lines of source code, with substantial tail of larger systems. Across the 10,159 instances with successful test parsing, the verifier contains 2.09 million statically identified test definitions, providing dense coverage at the instance level. Because these tests are inherited from the source repositories, they exercise behavior across the public interface rather than checking only few end to end outcomes. Success therefore depends on implementing coherent repository whose components remain consistent under extensive verification. Repository Scale and Interaction diversity. The environments and trajectories capture sustained development at the repository level. The median oracle repository contains 26 source files, and the median SFT trajectory contains 64 assistant turns, as shown in Figure 2(c). successful trajectory must keep track of multi-file project while successive edits are implemented and tested. Together, the long-horizon trajectories and varied operations provide rich supervision for maintaining project state as agents coordinate changes across files and refine their implementations through execution feedback. Implementation Scope. Figure 2(d) shows the distribution of implementation scope and its relationship with reconstruction performance. We measure each environments success rate as the fraction of teacher trajectories receiving full reward. Environments with matched trajectories are ordered by and divided into five equally sized groups, whose mean scope and success rates are plotted in the lower panel. Mean success falls from 23.0% in the group with the smallest scope to 13.4% in the group with the largest. This trend supports as proxy for the demands of repository reconstruction.

SWE-bench Verified (Jimenez et al., 2024), SWE-bench Pro (Deng et al., 2025), and SWE-bench Multilingual (Zan et al., 2025) assess the ability to resolve issues in existing repositories, while Terminal-Bench 2.1 (Merrill et al., 2026) evaluates task completion in terminal environments. Together, these benchmarks measure coding-agent performance across both project construction and repository maintenance. Evaluation Settings. We use Claude Code version 2.1.140 as the agent scaffold. The maximum context length is 262,144 tokens, and the maximum output length is 32,768 tokens. Context is automatically compacted when its usage reaches 80% of the maximum context length. For decoding, we set temperature to 1.0, top-p to 0.95, and top-k to 20. 5.2 Main Results Table 1 compares RepoHorizen-35B-A3B and its base model with representative closed-source and open-weight models. On NL2Repo, which directly evaluates full-repository reconstruction, training raises the score from 23.8 to 46.4, gain of 22.6 points. This is the strongest listed result among open-weight models below 200B parameters. RepoHorizen also surpasses GPT-5.5 and Gemini-3.1 Pro, which score 45.1 and 33.4, respectively, as well as larger open-weight models DeepSeek-V4Pro and MiniMax-M3, which score 38.5 and 42.1. Improvements extend to all four remaining benchmarks, with gains of 1.3 to 6.8 points across issue resolution and cross-domain long-horizon tasks in Terminal-Bench 2.1. These results suggest that RepoFactory training transfers beyond repository generation to broader software engineering and terminal work at fixed model scale. Environment evolution further strengthens this performance across all five benchmarks, adding 5.1 points on NL2Repo and 2.1 points on average over the no-evolution variant. These additional gains support the effectiveness of our proxy metrics in guiding environment evolution that improve training value. 5.3 Environment Scaling Figure 3: Average accuracy as function of the number of RepoFactory training environments. Figure 3 shows how NL2Repo performance changes as the training set grows. Performance increases steadily from 23.8% without RepoFactory environments to 46.4% with 5,577 environments, consistent with the 22.6-point gain reported in Table 1. The improvement continues at the largest scale tested, with no evidence of saturation. The gains become more pronounced beyond 3,000 environments. Adding the remaining 2,577 environments raises performance from 36.5% to 46.4%, suggesting that the larger collection exposes the model to repository structures and behavioral requirements that smaller subsets do not cover. sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented RepoFactory, an automated pipeline that constructs verifiable environments for fullrepository generation from real-world projects. Its Environment Evolution Loop uses timely, lowcost feedback to optimize validity, implementation scope, and structural coupling, recovering failed conversions and improving task value. The resulting 10,159 environments span 17 software domains. Training Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on these environments yields RepoHorizen-35B-A3B, with gains of 22.6 percentage points on NL2RepoBench and 8.5 points on average across five coding and agentic benchmarks. Environment evolution contributes further 5.1 and 2.1 points over training without evolution. These findings highlight the value of repository-level environments for coding-agent training and support low-cost proxy objectives as practical means of improving their training value at scale. Figure 6: Cumulative number of validated environments over wall-clock time, sampled every 30 minutes. To assess whether optimizing and improves training value, we run two independent evolution experiments from the same 1,000 randomly sampled environments. Each experiment targets one metric while retaining validity checks. We collect environments after rounds 3, 6, 9, and 12 as Levels 1 through 4, respectively. Each level supplies 2,000 trajectories for fine-tuning Qwen3.5-35BA3B with the same initialization and optimization settings. As shown in Figure 5, optimizing produces longer interactions and contexts and more supervised tokens. NL2Repo accuracy increases steadily from 30.2% at Level 1 to 32.9% at Level 4. Expanding implementation scope thus provides more extensive development experience within fixed number of trajectories, accompanied by improved reconstruction performance. sections.title: 7 Limitations
sections.content: RepoFactory currently focuses on Python projects, with relatively limited coverage of other programming languages. Our proxy metrics provide useful, low-cost guidance for environment evolution, but characterize task content at broad structural level. They do not yet explicitly distinguish the capabilities required by individual tasks. Extending language coverage and incorporating more detailed information about these capability requirements could support wider range of development settings and more targeted training.

sections.title: A Implementation Details
sections.content: This appendix describes the trajectory preparation and supervised fine-tuning configuration used for Qwen3.5-35B-A3B. A.1 Trajectory Filtering and Cleaning Before fine-tuning, we retain trajectories with rewards above 0.5 and apply offline quality checks. Deterministic checks examine record validity, dialogue structure, consistency between tool calls and results, response completeness, and the formatting of reasoning and code. They also screen for repetition, interaction loops, contamination, potentially sensitive or harmful content, and attempts to obtain information outside the intended task environment. We discard trajectories with clear violations and flag ambiguous cases for review. language-model judge reviews the flagged trajectories. These trajectories are included in the SFT data only when the judge determines that the apparent violation is benign. Confirmed violations and unresolved cases remain excluded. A.2 SFT Hyperparameters Hyperparameter Value We fine-tune the model, using the settings in Table 3. The data are shuffled during training, with no online generation. Following the Qwen3.5 multiturn objective, we compute the loss over assistant spans, including tool calls. System, user, and toolresult turns provide context but receive no loss. The rollout and global batch sizes are both 64, and the per-device micro-batch size is 1. Dynamic token batching limits each GPU to 80,000 tokens, with no separate sequence-length cap. Tensor, context, and expert parallel sizes are 2, 4, and 8, respectively. Sequence parallelism is enabled, while pipeline and expert tensor parallel sizes are both 1. We use AdamW with weight decay of 0.1 and coefficients β1 = 0.9 and β2 = 0.98. The learning rate warms up to 1.0 106 over the first 10% of training, then decays to 1.0 107 following cosine schedule.

Figure 7 summarizes the estimated coverage of Python ecosystems across RepoFactorys 10,159 environments. The estimates use the available Python repository records. We assign ecosystem labels by matching direct runtime dependency names trajectories, alongside frequent workspace exploration and code modification. Inline Python execution appears in 88.2% of trajectories, assertion or diff checks in 78.0%, and test-suite execution in 33.2%. These activities provide supervision for both implementing project code and examining its behavior through execution and local checks. against predefined rules. For repositories without dependency-based match, we use ecosystem terms in the first substantive paragraph of the project description. An environment may belong to multiple categories. Validation and serialization are the most common category at 32.7%, followed by HTTP, networking, and asynchronous tooling at 28.6%. Numerical computing, command-line tools, text processing, and data analysis are also widely represented. The distribution extends from common application infrastructure to specialized scientific libraries, web frameworks, and machine-learning frameworks, covering range of software stacks for repository reconstruction.
